articles.title: Mother Hubbard Opens in Middleton Shopping Centre with 45p Fish and Chips Offer
articles.excerpt: Hundreds queued for hours at the opening of Mother Hubbard's Fish and Chips in Middleton, where meals were offered for just 45p to celebrate the new store's launch.
articles.content_html:
ONGOING STORY — Updated 13 September 2026 at 10:57. 3 source updates have been combined into this article.

Mother Hubbard opened its new branch in Middleton Shopping Centre on 12 September 2026, offering a special promotion of 45p fish and chips for the first 1,000 customers. This opening drew significant crowds, with customers queuing back to the bus station to take advantage of the offer.

Among the first to enjoy the new menu was Colin Thompson, who praised the food and the hard work of the staff on social media. Other customers expressed their excitement and support for the new establishment, highlighting the positive reception it received in the community.

The opening of Mother Hubbard coincided with a busy day for the nearby Middleton Fish Bar, which reported selling out of its stock and closing early at 2.30pm due to high demand. Owners Paul and Caroline High thanked their customers for their support and engagement on social media, reflecting the thriving fish and chip trade in the area.

The successful launch of Mother Hubbard and the strong performance of Middleton Fish Bar indicate a vibrant market for fish and chips in Middleton, suggesting that local residents have a keen appetite for this traditional takeaway option.

articles.title: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark Perform First Concert in Rochdale After 47 Years
articles.excerpt: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark (OMD) performed their first concert in Rochdale on 7 August 2026, alongside Peter Hook & The Light and A Certain Ratio, marking a significant homecoming for the band.
articles.content_html:
Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark (OMD) made a historic return to Rochdale on 7 August 2026, performing their first-ever concert in the town at Rochdale Town Hall Square. The event, part of their Summer of Hits tour, also featured performances from Peter Hook & The Light and A Certain Ratio, drawing a crowd of over 5,000 music fans.

The concert was particularly significant as it marked 47 years since OMD recorded their debut single "Electricity" at the now-legendary Cargo Studios in Rochdale. This studio has been pivotal in the history of British music, hosting recordings from influential bands such as Joy Division and A Certain Ratio, making the event a true homecoming for OMD.

The evening was characterised by a vibrant atmosphere, with attendees donning Joy Division shirts and celebrating the rich musical heritage of the area. A Certain Ratio opened the night with a dynamic set that included tracks like "Do the Du" and their interpretation of Talking Heads' "Houses in Motion," setting a lively tone for the evening.

The concert not only celebrated OMD's past but also highlighted the ongoing relevance of the bands involved. With Rochdale Town Hall illuminated by the summer sun, the event was a fitting tribute to the town's musical legacy and a memorable night for all who attended.

A man has been charged with firearm and driving offences following a police pursuit in Heywood on Thursday, 10 September. Christopher Riley, aged 49, of New Line, Bacup, faces charges of possession of a firearm, dangerous driving, and failing to stop for police.

The incident began when officers received intelligence regarding a potential firearm inside a vehicle. Police pursued the suspect vehicle, leading to the charges against Riley.

Riley has been remanded in custody and is scheduled to appear at Manchester and Salford Magistrates' Court today, Saturday, 12 September.

This case highlights ongoing police efforts to address firearm-related incidents and ensure public safety in the area.

articles.title: Maggie’s Oldham to Host Annual Culture Crawl from Oldham to Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Culture Crawl on September 26 invites locals to walk 10k from Oldham to Rochdale, raising funds for Maggie’s Oldham, which supports cancer patients and their families.
articles.content_html:
Maggie’s Oldham is inviting locals to participate in its annual Culture Crawl on Saturday, September 26, aimed at raising funds for the centre that supports individuals living with cancer and their families. This year, the 10-kilometre walk will start in Oldham and for the first time will finish at the iconic Rochdale Town Hall.

Participants will have the opportunity to explore local history, culture, and community spirit along the route, which promises to be a memorable day for individuals, families, and teams. The event will feature various stops where walkers can enjoy local entertainment and food, enhancing the community experience.

Registration for the Culture Crawl will begin at 12pm at The Loom in Oldham, with walkers setting off shortly after. Sharon Furlong, whose husband has received support from Maggie’s Oldham, expressed the significance of the event, stating, “Taking part in Maggie’s Culture Crawl this year means so much to me.”

Every penny raised during the event will go directly towards supporting those affected by cancer, making it a vital fundraising effort for the local community. Participants are encouraged to sign up and contribute to this important cause.

articles.title: Festival of Remembrance Scheduled for Rochdale Town Hall on 16 October
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Town Hall will host a Festival of Remembrance on 16 October, organised by the council and local veterans, to honour the Armed Forces community and raise funds for local charities.
articles.content_html:
A Festival of Remembrance will take place at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday, 16 October, to honour members of the Armed Forces community. The event is organised by Rochdale Borough Council in collaboration with local veterans' groups and aims to recognise the service and sacrifice of both past and present Armed Forces personnel.

The evening will feature performances by military bands, an act of remembrance, and the sharing of historic war stories. Dignitaries expected to attend include the Mayor of Rochdale, MPs, councillors, and representatives from the Armed Forces. Mayor Faisal Rana expressed that this event will be a significant occasion for the Armed Forces community to unite and pay respect to those who have served.

Tickets for the event are priced at £15, which includes a pie and pea supper. Proceeds from the evening will support the Mayor of Rochdale’s charities for 2026 and 2027, which include the Rochdale Veterans Breakfast Club, Rochdale Women’s Welfare Association, SANDS (Stillbirth and Neonatal Death Society), Springhill Hospice, and The Christie.

This Festival of Remembrance marks the first such event since 2019, making it a poignant gathering for the community. Attendees are encouraged to reflect on the contributions of the Armed Forces while enjoying a night of remembrance and camaraderie.

articles.title: NEMA Launches Next-Generation Aerospace Technology from Rochdale
articles.excerpt: NEMA, a Rochdale-based aerospace firm, is advancing the industry with innovative technologies aimed at improving efficiency and reducing environmental impact in aviation.
articles.content_html:
NEMA, a Rochdale-based aerospace company, is set to enhance the aviation industry with its latest advancements in aerospace technology. Established in 1954 as The Nordale Spring Company, NEMA has evolved significantly over the decades, changing its name in 2003 to Nordale Electro-Mechanical Actuation. The firm has built a reputation for designing and manufacturing precision-engineered motors, generators, and components, primarily for the aerospace and defence sectors.

Operating from the Chichester Business Centre, NEMA is recognised as one of the UK's leading specialists in high-performance aerospace components. The company provides comprehensive engineering solutions, from concept development and prototyping to qualification, production, and aftermarket support. This approach ensures that advanced aerospace technologies are brought into service with confidence, catering to a global clientele.

A key focus for NEMA is the development of electrification technologies that support the aviation sector's transition towards more-electric and hybrid-electric aircraft. These innovations aim to improve operational efficiency, reduce weight, enhance reliability, and lower the environmental impact of aviation, aligning with industry goals for sustainability.

The firm has received support from the Rochdale Development Agency throughout its journey, contributing to its growth and prominence in the advanced manufacturing sector. As NEMA continues to innovate, it is helping to position Rochdale on the global map for advanced aerospace manufacturing.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real and much‑loved spot in Healey Dell — but its supernatural stories belong to the region’s folklore, not its archives.
articles.summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real and much‑loved spot in Healey Dell — but its supernatural stories belong to the region’s folklore, not its archives.
articles.body:
Ask any walker who’s slipped down the steep steps to the riverside at Healey Dell and you’ll get the same mixture of delight and bemusement: a narrow rocky cleft that looks, if you squint, a little like a chapel, and a name — the Fairies’ Chapel — that invites imagination. The place is part of a managed nature reserve with a heritage centre and tea rooms; its landscape is the product of geology, industry and decades of storytelling. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The feature people call the Fairies’ Chapel sits in a gorge known locally as “the Thrutch”, where the River Spodden squeezes through rock to make falls and pools. Erosion has hollowed niches and smooth grooves that earlier visitors likened to benches and a pulpit carved in stone — an entirely natural effect of the water working the sandstone over centuries. Local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre explain the physical origin of the name alongside the site’s visitor attractions for families. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

The documented history of the Dell is straightforward and well recorded. The valley contains the remains of water‑powered mills and reservoirs; a disused nineteenth‑century railway line now forms a trail; and the high viaduct that dominates the view is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. These are matters of record: industrial archaeology, recorded listing details and the council’s nature‑reserve management form the verifiable backbone of Healey Dell’s story. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The fairy stories are a different matter. The best‑known written version of the Fairies’ Chapel tale appears in John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (1829–31), a collection of local romances and folk narratives that includes a dramatic account involving a miller, Lady Eleanor (a Byron), enchanted gatherings and a Fairy Queen. Roby’s work preserves how nineteenth‑century readers and storytellers cast the Dell, but it is a literary record of folklore rather than archival evidence of historical events. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Folklore collectors and later guides have mixed motifs — fairies, witches, a Fairy King, even a Robin Hood‑like figure in some retellings — so you will find several versions in print and on local heritage pages. These stories are culturally valuable: they tell us how people have related to the landscape, explained strange rock shapes and given meaning to the place. But none of the dramatic supernatural claims in the tales (for example, fairies turning witches to stone or prophetic fairy queens) are backed by independent documentary records; they survive in oral tradition and literary retelling. If a claim cannot be verified in parish records, legal documents or contemporary reports, it should be treated as folklore. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

One concrete historical note helps show how the Dell changed: nineteenth‑century guides and more recent heritage material point to a major storm and flood on 4 July 1838 that altered sections of the Spodden and the features visitors once saw. Floods and later human activity mean the rocks and cavities admired by earlier writers are not exactly as they were, which helps explain differences between story and present‑day topography. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

So: are there fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean tiny supernatural beings recorded by contemporary evidence — no. If you mean a place where natural rock formations, industrial remnants and 150‑plus years of storytelling meet and feed the imagination — very much yes. The Fairies’ Chapel is best enjoyed on two levels: look closely at the geology and the listed structures that are historically verifiable, and then listen to the old tales (Roby and later local guides are the main published sources) as a living part of local culture. Both make Healey Dell worth a visit. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Man Arrested for Immigration Offences at Old Middleton Cemetery
articles.excerpt: A man has been arrested for immigration offences after three tents were discovered at Old Middleton Cemetery, prompting police investigations and community outreach efforts.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

19:51, 13 September 2026

A man has been arrested for immigration offences after three tents were discovered at Old Middleton Cemetery, prompting police investigations and community outreach efforts.

A man has been arrested for immigration offences following the discovery of three tents at Old Middleton Cemetery on September 11, 2026. The arrest was made after police were alerted to the situation during a multi-agency meeting, as reported by Middleton Labour.

The tents were occupied by three individuals, two of whom were described as white British. Following the arrest, the other two occupants were offered temporary accommodation but declined the offer. The council's rough sleepers outreach team had been assisting these individuals for several weeks and will continue to provide support.

In addition to the police response, Rochdale Council's Environmental Management Team has been deployed to the cemetery to clear rubbish, litter, and damaged bins, as well as to remove the abandoned tents. Strimming work has also commenced at the site to improve its condition.

The tents were reportedly slashed overnight after social media posts labelled the area as a 'migrant camp'. Police are investigating this incident and have appealed for information regarding the vandalism. They are also monitoring social media for comments that may incite violence, urging anyone experiencing hate crime or racial abuse to report it to the authorities.
